Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration creates an AWS resource without encryption at rest.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration creates an AWS resource without encryption at rest.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Encryption at rest is not enabled. This exposes data to unauthorized access and potential theft.
Description.Recommendations: Enforce encryption of sensitive data at rest.

Reference.Title: AWS Well-Architected Framework Security Pillar
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services, Inc. or its affiliates

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS Terraform Misconfiguration: Insecure EBS Storage

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration creates an AWS resource with insufficient transport layer protection.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration creates an AWS resource with insufficient transport layer protection.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Connections to the AWS resources are insecure. These insecure connections expose data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering.
Description.Recommendations: Use a secure transport protocol to protect data in transit.

Reference.Title: Protecting data in transit
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services, Inc. or its affiliates

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS Terraform Misconfiguration: Insecure ElastiCache Transport

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration creates a publicly accessible AWS resource.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration creates a publicly accessible AWS resource.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Publicly accessible resources are susceptible to distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks and expose data to unauthorized access and potential theft.
Description.Recommendations: Block public access to AWS resources that store sensitive data.

Reference.Title: Enforce access control
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services, Inc. or its affiliates

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS Terraform Misconfiguration: Redshift Publicly Accessible

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration does not specify a customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.<AltParagraph>A configuration does not specify a customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Customer-managed keys are not used to encrypt data at rest.
By default, AWS uses AWS-managed keys to encrypt data at rest if encryption is enabled. Customer-managed keys enable organizations to use cryptographic keys of their choice to encrypt data. This gives organizations better control over and logging of encryption processes.
As such, customer-managed keys are often part of the solution to address requirements that include but are not limited to: - Audit logs for sensitive data access - Data residency - Replacing, disabling, or destroying keys
Note that keys with the format aws/service-name are reserved for AWS-managed keys.
Description.Recommendations:
For more control over the encryption process of sensitive data, configure customer-managed keys to encrypt data at rest.
Using customer-managed keys requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation.
Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Reference.Title: AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services, Inc. or its affiliates

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Backup Missing Customer-Managed Encryption Key

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration does not apply proper access controls.<AltParagraph>A configuration does not apply proper access controls.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Publicly accessible resources are susceptible to distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks and expose data to unauthorized access, tampering, and potential theft.
Description.Recommendations: Block public access to AWS resources that store sensitive data.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: AmazonMQ Publicly Accessible

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Azure SQL Database does not enable data encryption.<AltParagraph>An Azure SQL Database does not enable data encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Physical media theft is a common means for attackers to gain access to confidential information. By default, Azure SQL Databases use Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) to encrypt and protect data at rest. Disabling TDE for an Azure SQL Database exposes the data to potential theft. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Azure SQL Database that does not encrypt its data. 
resource "azurerm_mssql_database" "aztf008-tp-01" {
  name           = "aztf008-db-d"
  ... 
  sku_name       = "DW100c"
  ...
  transparent_data_encryption_enabled = false
}
Description.Recommendations:
By default, Azure SQL Database instances are encrypted with Transparent Data Encryption (TDE). Transparent Data Encryption should be enabled to protect the data at rest. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Azure SQL Database with Transparent Data Encryption enabled. 
resource "azurerm_mssql_database" "aztf008-tp-01" {
  name           = "aztf008-db-d"
  ... 
  sku_name       = "DW100c"
  ...
  transparent_data_encryption_enabled = true
}

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Azure Terraform Misconfiguration: Missing SQL Database Encryption

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, Azure SQL VM Auto Backup is not configured to encrypt backups.<AltParagraph>Azure SQL VM Auto Backup is not configured to encrypt backups.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Data backups are often over-looked as assets that require just as much protection as the original data. Unencrypted backups leave the backup data accessible to potential attackers. By default, Azure SQL Virtual Machines Automated Backup settings do not enforce encryption of data backups. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines Azure SQL Virtual Machine Automated Backup settings that do not enforce encryption of backup data. 
resource "azurerm_mssql_virtual_machine" "aztf009-tn-03" {
  virtual_machine_id               = data.azurerm_virtual_machine.example.id
  ...
  auto_backup {
    retention_period_in_days = 1
    storage_blob_endpoint = ""
    storage_account_access_key = azurerm_storage_account.example.primary_access_key
  }
}
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that data backups are protected from unauthorized access. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines Azure SQL Virtual Machine Automated Backup settings that enforce encryption of backup data. 
resource "azurerm_mssql_virtual_machine" "aztf009-tn-03" {
  virtual_machine_id               = data.azurerm_virtual_machine.example.id
  ...
  auto_backup {
    encryption_enabled = true
    retention_period_in_days = 1
    storage_blob_endpoint = ""
    storage_account_access_key = azurerm_storage_account.example.primary_access_key
}

Reference.Title: Automated Backup v2 for Azure virtual machines (Resource Manager)

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration defines a network rule with overly broad access permissions.<AltParagraph>A configuration defines a network rule with overly broad access permissions.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Loose access configurations can expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are typically subjected to near-continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities.
This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published, such as Heartbleed. Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit.
Description.Recommendations:
Define network rules that restrict access to services and ensure the services are available to as limited an audience as possible.
For example, do not make ports for service management activities publicly accessible. Ensure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Azure service does not use customer-managed keys.<AltParagraph>An Azure service does not use customer-managed keys.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Mismanaged encryption keys are the cause of various security breaches. Organizations should not rely on platform-managed keys for critical data resources.
Description.Recommendations:
By default, Azure leverages platform-managed keys (PMKs) to protect data.
Organizations can instead configure Azure services to use customer-managed keys (CMKs) to protect their data.
Specifically using CMKs enables organizations to:
- import HSM-generated keys - audit usage of keys - control access to keys - cancel, revoke, or rotate keys
Using CMKs requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation.
Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Azure service does not enable host-based encryption.<AltParagraph>An Azure service does not enable host-based encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Azure offers several encryption options, each with specific benefits and limitations. For example, Azure storage server-side encryption (SSE) performs encryption by default without using compute resources, however, it does not encrypt the temporary disk or caches. It also does not protect data flowing from a compute instance to storage. Azure Disk Encryption (ADE), encrypts both temporary disks and caches, as well as data flowing to storage, but at the expense of compute resources.
Description.Recommendations: Consider enabling host-based encryption for resources that support this encryption option. Encryption at host (or host-based encryption) provides end-to-end data encryption. It utilizes the underlying VM host to encrypt data before the data flows to Azure Storage. Encryption at host does not use the guest VM's CPU and consequently does not impact its performance.

Reference.Title: Overview of managed disk encryption options
Reference.Author: Microsoft

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Azure Terraform Misconfiguration: AKS Cluster Missing Host-Based Encryption

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Azure service does not enable infrastructure encryption.<AltParagraph>An Azure service does not enable infrastructure encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Implementation flaws, misconfigurations, and compromised keys are some of the problems that prevent single-layer encryption from fully protecting highly-sensitive data. Organizations should adopt a defense-in-depth approach to protect highly-sensitive data and avoid having a single-point-of-failure in their security design.
Description.Recommendations: Consider enabling infrastructure encryption to protect highly-sensitive data. Organizations should choose protection measures appropriate to the classification of the data in question. Azure infrastructure encryption typically leverages separate platform-managed keys as an added measure of safety, and is performed at the layer closest to the storage or network interfaces. Most Azure services provide service-level encryption by default. Enabling infrastructure encryption enforces a second layer of encryption, thus protecting the data with double encryption. Because the data is encrypted twice, performance might be degraded. Consequently, organizations should use a risk-driven approach to determine whether infrastructure encryption is needed.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration does not apply proper access controls.<AltParagraph>A configuration does not apply proper access controls.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Uncontrolled access to critical or sensitive resources can significantly impact an organization in various ways, including disclosure of or tampering with critical data.

When changing access controls, identify all dependent systems to limit potential disruptions.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration sets an overly permissive CORS policy.<AltParagraph>A configuration sets an overly permissive CORS policy.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a technology that allows a domain to define a policy for its resources to be accessed by a web page hosted on a different domain. Historically, web browsers have restricted their domain resources from being accessed by scripts loaded from a different domain to abide by the same origin policy. CORS provides a method for a domain to safelist other domains and allow them to access its resources.
Be careful when defining a CORS policy because an overly permissive policy configured at the server level for a domain or a directory on a domain can expose more content for cross-domain access than intended. CORS can enable a malicious application to communicate with a victim application inappropriately, leading to information disclosure, spoofing, data theft, relay, or other attacks.
Implementing CORS can increase an application's attack surface and should only be used when necessary.
Description.Recommendations: Do not use a wildcard (*) as the value for the allowedOrigins property. Instead, provide an explicit list of trusted domains.

Description.Explanation: Insufficiently protected data communication channels can put critical organizational data at risk of theft, tampering, or disclosure.

Transport protection mechanisms include measures such as: - Enforcing encrypted communication - Using robust encryption algorithms - Using the latest known-secure version of communication protocols - Protecting the integrity of data in transit

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the configuration defines a service with insufficient audit logging.<AltParagraph>The template defines a service with insufficient audit logging.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
A lack of audit records limits the ability to detect and respond to security-related incidents and prevents forensic investigation.
Configuration settings that undermine logging capabilities include but are not limited to: - deliberately disabling audit logging - exempting actions of specific users, groups, or processes from being logged - inadequately protecting log integrity - not enabling optional audit logging - reducing the log sampling rate
Description.Recommendations: Enable audit logging for all security-sensitive services. Capture logs for all users without exemption.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration sets up a resource that lacks monitoring.<AltParagraph>A configuration sets up a resource that lacks monitoring.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Any delayed response to breaches undermines an organization's ability to limit the impact of a breach.
Configuration settings that undermine monitoring capabilities include but are not limited to: - deliberately disabling monitoring - not enabling optional monitoring - not specifying relevant events to export to monitoring services - exempting actions of specific users, groups, processes, and geographical regions from monitoring
Description.Recommendations: Leverage breach detection controls to detect and respond quickly to attacks.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration does not specify a customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.<AltParagraph>A configuration does not specify a customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Customer-managed keys are not used to encrypt data at rest.
Customer-managed keys enable organizations to use cryptographic keys of their choice to encrypt data. This gives organizations better control over encryption processes.
As such, customer-managed keys are often part of the solution to address requirements that include but are not limited to: - Audit logs for sensitive data access - Data residency - Replacing, disabling, or destroying keys
Description.Recommendations:
For more control over the encryption process of sensitive data, configure customer-managed keys to encrypt data at rest.
Using customer-managed keys requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation.
Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Description.Explanation:

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration does not specify any customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration does not specify any customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are not enabled for data at rest.
By default, Google Cloud uses randomly generated Data Encryption Keys (DEK) to encrypt data at rest. The CMEK feature allows organizations to use cryptographic keys of their choice to encrypt DEK. This gives organizations better control over and logging of encryption processes.
As such, CMEK is often part of the solution to address requirements that include but are not limited to: - Audit logs for sensitive data access - Data residency - Replacing, disabling, or destroying keys - Tamper-resistant hardware security module
Description.Recommendations:
For greater control over the encryption process of sensitive data, configure a Cloud KMS key to protect Data Encryption Keys (DEK) that encrypt data at rest.
Using customer-managed keys requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation.
Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Amazon EBS volumes are unencrypted by default. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates an EBS volume. The EBS volume is unencrypted because the encrypted argument is set to false. 
resource "aws_ebs_volume" "demo_ebs" {
...
  encrypted = false
...
}

Amazon EBS volumes and snapshots are unencrypted by default unless there is a region-wide setting to enforce EBS resource encryption. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that disables the default EBS resource encryption by setting the enabled argument to false. 
resource "aws_ebs_encryption_by_default" "demo_default" {
  enabled = false
}

Amazon EBS snapshots are unencrypted by default. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that makes an unencrypted copy of an EBS snapshot by setting the encrypted argument to false. 
resource "aws_ebs_snapshot_copy" "copy_demo" {
...
  encrypted = false
...
}

Amazon EBS snapshots are unencrypted by default. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that imports a disk file as an unencrypted EBS snapshot by setting the encrypted argument to false. 
resource "aws_ebs_snapshot_import" "import_demo" {
...
  encrypted = false
...
}

By default, Amazon RDS does not encrypt database instances before saving data in the underlying storage. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates a database instance without storage encryption by setting the storage_encrypted argument to false. 
resource "aws_db_instance" "demo_instance" {
...
  storage_encrypted = false
...
}

By default, Amazon RDS does not encrypt read replicas before saving data in the underlying storage. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates an Amazon RDS read replica without storage encryption. The kms_key_id argument that specifies the AWS KMS key to encrypt replica data at rest is commented out. 
resource "aws_db_instance" "demo_instance" {
...
  replicate_source_db = "demo-db"
  # kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:111122223333:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab"
...
}

By default, Amazon SNS does not encrypt messages before saving them to disk. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates an SNS topic without storage encryption. The kms_master_key_id argument that specifies the AWS KMS key to encrypt messages is commented out. 
resource "aws_sns_topic" "demo_sns_topic" {
  name = "demo-sns-topic"
  # kms_master_key_id = "alias/aws/sns"
}

Amazon ElastiCache in-transit encryption is an optional feature to enforce encrypted and authenticated connections to ElastiCache resources. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates an ElastiCache replication group without enforcing in-transit encryption because the transit_encryption_enabled argument is set to false. 
resource "aws_elasticache_replication_group" "demo_group" {
...
  transit_encryption_enabled = false
...
}
Example 2: The following example shows a configuration that defines an aws_elasticache_replication_group resource with transit_encryption_enabled unset. 
resource "aws_elasticache_replication_group" "demo_group" {
...
  # MISSING transit_encryption_enabled ...
...
}

By default, an RDS Proxy does not encrypt the network traffic between the client application and the database. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates an RDS Proxy without enforcing TLS connections because the require_tls argument is set to false. 
resource "aws_db_proxy" "demo_proxy" {
...
  require_tls  = false
...
}

By default, Amazon Redshift blocks connections from outside of the virtual network that hosts the cluster's subnets. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that creates an Amazon Redshift cluster. The cluster allows public access because the publicly_accessible argument is set to true. 
resource "aws_redshift_cluster" "demo_cluster" {
...
  publicly_accessible = true
...
}

Amazon API Gateway exposes backend HTTP endpoints, AWS Lambda functions, and other AWS services through a collection of routes and methods. Routes and methods that lack authorization control could be publicly accessible. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an HTTP method for an API Gateway resource. The method has no access control because the authorization argument is set to NONE. 
resource "aws_api_gateway_method" "demo_method" {
...

Amazon API Gateway exposes backend HTTP endpoints, AWS Lambda functions, and other AWS services through a collection of routes and methods. Routes and methods for APIs that lack authorization control could be publicly accessible. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Amazon API Gateway Version 2 route. The APIs have no access control because the authorization_type argument is set to NONE. 
resource "aws_apigatewayv2_route" "demo_route" {
...
  authorization_type = "NONE"
...
}
Example 2: The following example shows a configuration that defines an Amazon API Gateway Version 2 route resource with authorization_type unset. 
resource "aws_apigatewayv2_route" "demo_route" {
...
  # MISSING authorization_type ...
...
}

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters do not leverage host-based encryption by default. Host-based encryption uses the VM host of the AKS agent nodes' VMs to encrypt data at rest, which then flows encrypted to the Storage service. Consult your organizational policies and determine whether host-based encryption is needed. Example 2: The following example improves the configuration in Example 1. It enables host-based encryption for the AKS cluster by setting the enable_host_encryption property in the default_node_pool block to true. 
resource "azurerm_kubernetes_cluster" "aztf017-tn-01" {
  name                = "example-aks1"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters do not leverage host-based encryption by default. Host-based encryption uses the VM host of the AKS agent nodes' VMs to encrypt data at rest, which then flows encrypted to the Storage service. Consult your organizational policies and determine whether host-based encryption is needed. Example 2: The following example improves the configuration in Example 1. It enables host-based encryption for the AKS cluster by setting the enable_host_encryption property in the default_node_pool block to true. 
resource "azurerm_kubernetes_cluster_node_pool" "aztf017-tn-02" {

  name                  = "internal"
  kubernetes_cluster_id = azurerm_kubernetes_cluster.aztf017-tn-02.id
  vm_size               = "Standard_DS2_v2"
  node_count            = 1
  ...
}

resource "azurerm_linux_virtual_machine" "aztf018-tn-01" {

  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  ...
  encryption_at_host_enabled = true
  ...
}

Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. The cluster block specifies a CMEK stored in the Google Cloud KMS (kms_key_name) to protect DEK.

...

    cluster_id   = "demo-cluster"
    num_nodes    = 1
    storage_type = "HDD"
    kms_key_name = "projects/KMS_PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/keyRings/KEY_RING/cryptoKeys/KEY"
  }
...
}

dataset_id = "dataset_foobar"

  }
...
}

      }
    }

}
